title: Advanced agreement and notional concord
objectives: Identify the head of a complex subject.
Choose agreement for number expressions, proportions and measurements.
Interpret collective agreement and the reference of relative pronouns.

explanation.heading: Meaning and use
paragraphs: Subject–verb agreement is often straightforward: a singular subject takes a singular present-tense verb, and a plural subject takes a plural verb. In longer noun phrases, however, the word nearest the verb is not necessarily the head of the subject. In “The quality of the answers is improving”, quality is the head; answers belongs to a prepositional phrase.

Agreement can also follow how the speaker conceives a group. In British English, a collective noun such as committee or team may take a singular verb when the group is viewed as one body, or a plural verb when the members are prominent: “The committee has reached a decision” and “The committee are disagreeing among themselves.” Both patterns are possible; context and variety influence the choice.

explanation.heading: Form
paragraphs: A number of plus a plural noun normally takes a plural verb: “A number of applicants have withdrawn.” The number of plus a plural noun normally takes a singular verb: “The number of applicants has increased.” The expressions have different heads and meanings: a number of refers to several people or things, while the number of refers to a quantity.

Expressions of measurement can take a singular verb when a sum, period or distance is treated as a single amount: “Ten minutes is enough.” Some nouns ending in -s, such as news, normally take a singular verb. By contrast, plural-only nouns such as scissors normally take a plural verb, while “a pair of scissors” normally takes a singular verb.

explanation.heading: Examples in context
paragraphs: A relative clause can create a longer agreement chain. Compare “She is one of the researchers who work here” with “She is the only one of the researchers who works here.” In the first, who refers to researchers; in the second, who normally refers to the only one. The intended reference, and therefore the verb, differs.

With a proportion, agreement often depends on the noun after of: “Half of the equipment is ready” but “Half of the devices are ready.” In a formal report, check the noun being quantified instead of choosing a verb solely from half. Other quantities may behave differently according to meaning and construction.

explanation.heading: Contrasts and common mistakes
paragraphs: Do not label a British plural collective as wrong merely because its noun has no plural -s. Equally, a singular collective is appropriate when the group acts as a unit. Maintain a clear perspective across nearby verbs and pronouns, while recognising that a change of perspective can sometimes justify a change.

Avoid a plural verb merely because a plural noun appears between the head and the verb: “The list of participants is available.” Compare “A number of participants are waiting”, where a number of functions as a plural quantity expression. Both grammatical form and the intended referent matter.

examples.sentence: The list of participants is available.
examples.note: List is the singular head; participants is inside a prepositional phrase.

examples.sentence: A number of applicants have withdrawn.
examples.note: A number of refers to several applicants and normally takes a plural verb.

examples.sentence: The number of applicants has increased.
examples.note: The number refers to a quantity and takes a singular verb.

examples.sentence: The committee has reached its decision.
examples.note: The committee is presented as one body.

examples.sentence: The committee are disagreeing among themselves.
examples.note: British plural agreement foregrounds the members.

examples.sentence: Ten minutes is enough for the introduction.
examples.note: The period is treated as a single amount.

examples.sentence: Half of the equipment is ready.
examples.note: Equipment is uncountable here and takes singular agreement.

examples.sentence: She is one of the researchers who work here.
examples.note: Who refers to the plural researchers.

common_errors.incorrect: The quality of the responses are improving.
common_errors.correct: The quality of the responses is improving.
common_errors.reason: Quality is the singular head of the subject.

common_errors.incorrect: The number of applicants have increased.
common_errors.correct: The number of applicants has increased.
common_errors.reason: The number takes singular agreement in this construction.

common_errors.incorrect: The scissors is on the table.
common_errors.correct: The scissors are on the table.
common_errors.reason: Scissors is normally plural-only and takes a plural verb.

summary: Find the head of a complex subject before selecting the verb.
British collective nouns can take singular or plural agreement, depending on perspective.
Agreement with quantities and relative clauses depends on their structure and intended reference.

exercises.prompt: Which British sentence foregrounds the committee members as individuals?
exercises.explanation: Plural are and among themselves foreground the individual members in British usage.

options.text: The committee are one organisation and it has a name.
The committee are disagreeing among themselves.
The committee are an organisation with its own logo.
The committee is a single body called the panel.

option_feedback.a: “The committee are one organisation and it has a name.” does not fit here. Plural are and among themselves foreground the individual members in British usage.
option_feedback.b: “The committee are disagreeing among themselves.” fits here. Plural are and among themselves foreground the individual members in British usage.
option_feedback.c: “The committee are an organisation with its own logo.” does not fit here. Plural are and among themselves foreground the individual members in British usage.
option_feedback.d: “The committee is a single body called the panel.” does not fit here. Plural are and among themselves foreground the individual members in British usage.
